title: Dental unit waterlines & Legionella
blurb: Why biofilm grows in dental unit waterlines, the risk from Legionella, and the daily flushing and cleaning routine that keeps water safe.
question: It's the first appointment on Monday morning and the dentist asks you to get the surgery ready. What must you do with the dental unit waterlines before the first patient sits down, what do you repeat between patients, and why does it matter?

teach.body: Dental unit waterlines (DUWLs) are the narrow tubes that carry water to the handpieces, the three-in-one syringe and the ultrasonic scaler. Water sits still in them for long periods, at room temperature, with a huge surface area for its volume. Bacteria in the water stick to the inside walls and build a slimy layer called biofilm. The biofilm sheds microorganisms back into the water, which then reaches the patient's mouth and, as spray, the air everyone breathes.

teach.caption: Every quiet period (overnight, weekends, lunch breaks) lets the cycle speed up.

teach.body: Legionella bacteria cause Legionnaires' disease, a serious and sometimes fatal pneumonia. People catch it by breathing in tiny droplets of contaminated water, such as dental spray, not by drinking it. The bacteria thrive in still, lukewarm water (roughly 20–45 °C) and in biofilm. Every practice needs a Legionella risk assessment and a written scheme of control, following the Approved Code of Practice L8, which has special legal status. The Registered Manager is responsible for a safe water supply.

items.label: Flush all DUWLs for at least 2 minutes
e.g. after lunch: flush for at least 2 minutes
Flush for at least 2 minutes, then drain down. Remove the bottle, flush it with distilled or RO water, leave it open to dry overnight, stored upside down

teach.caption: Follow the manufacturer's protocol for daily cleaning too, and disinfect the lines periodically with the agent they recommend.

items.label: flush at start and end of day, and after breaks
the only water for self-contained bottles
expected bacterial count if water is tested

teach.caption: Routine testing with dip slides isn't essential unless the water tastes or smells wrong, and in-house test kits are not recommended.

teach.h: No single fix: a combination of controls
teach.body: HTM 01-05 says no single method completely removes contamination from DUWLs, so practices combine them. Flushing reduces the bacteria in the water at the moment patients are exposed, though it has only a small effect on biofilm itself. Periodic disinfection with the manufacturer's recommended agent tackles the biofilm, followed by thorough flushing before clinical use. Self-contained bottles use distilled or reverse osmosis (RO) water. In-line filters are cleaned at least at the end of each session, after flushing; disposable ones are replaced daily.

teach.note: Anti-retraction valves on handpieces, scalers and waterlines stop fluid from the patient's mouth being drawn back into the lines. They must be monitored and maintained.

teach.h: Bringing waterlines back after a closure
teach.caption: This applies where there is no manufacturer's guidance. During a closure, lines are flushed, drained and left disconnected, or flushed weekly if that isn't practical.

teach.text: Unit water is not sterile. For surgical procedures, such as raising a flap or irrigating into a body cavity, HTM 01-05 says use sterile water or sterile saline from a separate single-use source, not water from the dental unit.

items: Stagnant water in narrow DUWLs grows biofilm, which sheds microbes into the spray.
Legionella causes Legionnaires' disease, caught by inhaling contaminated aerosol.
Flush at least 2 minutes at start and end of day and after breaks; 20–30 seconds between patients.
Bottles: distilled or RO water; at night remove, flush, air-dry and store inverted.
No single fix: flushing plus periodic disinfection, maintenance and anti-retraction valves.

summary: You can now explain how biofilm forms in dental unit waterlines and why Legionella is a risk, carry out the HTM 01-05 flushing routine at the start and end of the day and between patients, look after self-contained water bottles, and explain why a combination of controls is needed.

A.q: According to HTM 01-05, how long should dental unit waterlines be flushed at the start of the working day?
A.why: HTM 01-05 says DUWLs should be flushed for at least two minutes at the beginning and end of the day and after significant periods without use.

whyNot.0: Ten seconds is too short for any HTM 01-05 flush.
whyNot.1: 20–30 seconds is the flush between patients.
whyNot.3: Fifteen minutes is not the HTM 01-05 figure.

A.q: How do people usually catch Legionnaires' disease?
options: Direct skin contact with an infected person
A needlestick injury from a used needle
A.why: Legionnaires' disease is caught by inhaling small droplets (aerosols) of water containing Legionella bacteria.

whyNot.0: Drinking is not the usual route; inhaling aerosols is.
whyNot.2: It is not normally spread from person to person.
whyNot.3: Needlestick injuries are linked with blood-borne viruses, not Legionella.

A.q: What should happen to a self-contained water bottle at the end of the day?
options: Top it up with tap water for the morning
Leave it attached and full overnight
Fill it with disinfectant and leave it attached overnight
Remove, flush, air-dry and store it upside down
A.why: HTM 01-05 says bottles are removed, flushed with distilled or RO water, left open to the air to dry overnight and stored inverted.

whyNot.0: Bottles use distilled or RO water, and are left empty and drying overnight.
whyNot.1: Leaving water standing overnight encourages biofilm.
whyNot.2: Disinfectants are used only as the manufacturer recommends, then flushed out before use.

B.q: How long should DUWLs be flushed between patients?
options: They don't need flushing between patients
B.why: HTM 01-05 says lines should be flushed for at least 20–30 seconds between patients.

whyNot.1: Two minutes is for the start and end of the day and after breaks.
whyNot.2: Five minutes is not an HTM 01-05 figure.
whyNot.3: Flushing between patients is part of the routine.

options: A protective film applied to new waterlines
A layer of bacteria stuck to the tube walls
Limescale left behind by hard water
B.why: Biofilm is a slimy layer of microorganisms that attaches to the inner surfaces of waterlines and sheds bacteria into the water.

whyNot.0: Biofilm is contamination, not something applied deliberately.
whyNot.2: Limescale is mineral deposit, not living bacteria.
whyNot.3: Biofilm is a microbial growth, not a disinfectant.

B.q: Which type of water should be used in a dental unit's self-contained bottle?
options: Water from the surgery hand basin
Water left over from the ultrasonic
B.why: HTM 01-05 says self-contained water supplies should use distilled or RO water.

whyNot.0: Hand-basin water isn't the specified quality and risks contamination.
whyNot.1: Mineral water isn't specified and can leave deposits.
whyNot.3: Ultrasonic solution is contaminated and must never be reused.

C.q: Which statement about flushing DUWLs is correct, according to HTM 01-05?
options: Flushing reduces counts but barely affects biofilm
Flushing is only needed once a week
Flushing fully replaces the need for periodic disinfection
C.why: HTM 01-05 notes flushing has only a small effect on biofilm build-up but usefully reduces counts in the water when patients are exposed, so it is combined with periodic disinfection.

whyNot.0: No single method completely removes contamination from DUWLs.
whyNot.2: Flushing is daily and between every patient.
whyNot.3: Periodic disinfection is still needed to tackle biofilm.

C.q: What is the purpose of anti-retraction valves on handpieces and scalers?
options: To keep the water at body temperature
To stop fluids being sucked back into lines
To filter Legionella bacteria out of the water
C.why: Anti-retraction valves provide backflow protection, preventing fluid from the patient's mouth being drawn back into the waterlines.

whyNot.1: They have nothing to do with water temperature.
whyNot.3: They prevent backflow; they are not bacterial filters.

C.q: The dentist is about to raise a surgical flap. What should be used for irrigation?
options: Sterile water or saline from a single-use source
Dental unit water that has just been flushed for 2 minutes
C.why: For surgical procedures involving flaps or access into body cavities, HTM 01-05 recommends sterile water or sterile saline from a separate single-use source.

whyNot.1: Unit water from the syringe is not sterile.
whyNot.2: Flushing reduces counts but doesn't make unit water sterile.
whyNot.3: Bottle water is distilled or RO, not sterile.

reteach.title: Think of a garden hose left in the sun
reteach.question: Ever turned on a garden hose that's been lying around for weeks and got a warm, slightly smelly first squirt? What's happening inside it?

blocks.h: The first squirt is the worst
blocks.body: Water left sitting in a hose warms up, and a slimy film grows on the inside. The first water out is the worst, so you let it run before filling a paddling pool. Dental waterlines are thin hoses that sit still every night and weekend. That's why you run them for at least 2 minutes first thing, and 20–30 seconds between patients. Running water clears what's floating in the line, but the slime on the walls needs regular disinfection too.

blocks.text: The risk isn't only swallowing the water: Legionella is caught by breathing in the fine spray from handpieces and syringes.

explain.body: Still water in narrow tubes lets bacteria stick to the walls and form biofilm, a slimy layer that sheds microbes into the water and spray reaching patients and staff.

test.q: Why do dental unit waterlines encourage biofilm?
options: The lines are made of glass
test.why: Long periods of stagnation in narrow-bore tubing with a large surface area let bacteria settle and form biofilm.

whyNot.1: Cold water actually slows bacterial growth.
whyNot.2: Waterlines are flexible tubing, and material isn't the main reason.
whyNot.3: Patients don't drink from the lines.

explain.body: Causes Legionnaires' disease, a serious pneumonia, caught by inhaling contaminated aerosol. Grows in still, lukewarm water and biofilm. Practices need a Legionella risk assessment and written scheme under ACoP L8.

test.q: Which document gives the Approved Code of Practice for controlling Legionella?
test.why: The Health and Safety Commission's Approved Code of Practice L8 covers the control of Legionella in water systems.

whyNot.2: IR(ME)R covers medical exposures to radiation.
whyNot.3: RIDDOR covers reporting injuries and dangerous occurrences.

explain.body: At least 2 minutes at the start and end of the day and after significant breaks; at least 20–30 seconds between patients.

test.q: You return from lunch to start the afternoon list. What should you do with the waterlines?
options: Nothing until the end of the day
test.why: After any significant period without use, such as a lunch break, HTM 01-05 says flush for at least two minutes.

whyNot.0: Lines that sat unused over lunch need flushing before patients.
whyNot.2: Five seconds is far too short.
whyNot.3: Overnight disinfection isn't the routine before an afternoon list.

explain.body: Bottles use distilled or RO water; at night remove, flush, air-dry, store inverted. Disinfect lines periodically with the manufacturer's agent and flush before use. Maintain anti-retraction valves and filters.

rows.label: Bottle filled from the hand basin
Bottle stored upside down to dry

test.q: After disinfecting the waterlines with the manufacturer's recommended agent, what must happen before patient use?
options: Leave the disinfectant in all day
test.why: HTM 01-05 says DUWLs must be thoroughly flushed after disinfection and before being returned to clinical use.

whyNot.0: Residual disinfectant mustn't reach patients unless the manufacturer specifies continuous dosing.
whyNot.2: Diluting doesn't remove it from the lines.
whyNot.3: The sterilizer has nothing to do with waterlines.
